Our GHC inventory is a critical tool in monitoring our progress. It works like a financial statement looking at the past to see whether we are on track or not or not on meeting our GHC reduction targets.

Carbon budgets offer a different weight to plan ahead and measure progress to our climate and GHG reduction targets.

A carbon budget sets the total amount of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions permitted over a period usually with milestones in 2030 and 2050 to stay within a temperature threshold of either 1.5 or 2 degrees Celsius.
It can then be broken down by year or budget cycle.
Carbon budgets are forward looking, meaning emissions of the activities of the municipality are estimated for the year or period ahead and then those projections are used to make decisions.
Carbon budgets mimic financial budgets by setting an upper limit of the amount of carbon available to emit.
If that amount is exceeded in one year it must be made up in another year.
By integrating the carbon budget into the financial budget.
Everyone.

Business Unit becomes responsible for considering and meeting the carbon budget. It can carbon budgets are calculated by considering the total global carbon budget available and what the fair allocation is for a city like Saskatoon. Cities with high GDP and high emissions are requested to reduce emissions rapidly while other cities can increase emissions in the short term. To meet a 1.5 degree warming threshold, all cities will need to be net zero by 2050.

Edmonton calculated their carbon budget based on an allowable 3.2 tons per person by 2030 and 0 tons per person by 2050. These per capita amounts used C40 cities recommendations to allocate a fair portion to cities based on the historic emissions and GDP as a discussed in the last slide.
Since Edmonton like Saskatoon has historically high emissions and high GDP, they need to reduce emissions quickly between now and 2030 with a plan to get to net zero by 2050.

Using this approach with their population projections, they determined that their total carbon budget was 155 million tons of CO2. They broke that down further to show the trajectory to get there and how many emissions they could emit every single year.
Since they have a four year budget cycle, they then determined the amount of emissions per cycle starting with 66.7 million tons of CO2 equivalents between 2019 and 2022.
Now that the carbon budget is set in Edmonton, they are now working to implement it by integrating it into their financial budgeting process.
They plan to identify the carbon impacts of their base budgets as well as the incremental increase and decrease with new budget requests such as new service packages or capital projects.

They understand that some areas will be easier to quantify than others and will start and plan to start with areas of GHD accounting strength and move to those more challenging areas as the budget process matures.
This figure shows their process starting with a number one where a project is identified for funding in the budget cycle.
Second, a carbon accounting tool is used to estimate the GHG impacts for the project.
Third, projects are prioritized for funding based on their GHG emissions impacts during budget deliberations.
Fourth, the carbon surplus or deficit is identified. If there is a deficit, I am going over the total allowed emissions for that year.
Then a city council report describing that deficit and how it will be rectified along the public hearing is required.
Finally, an evaluation of the impacts of actual emissions is compared to the budget using GHG inventories.
In order to implement a carbon budget in Saskatoon, principles would need to be agreed upon.

The following principles for development and implementation of a carbon budget and accounting framework could include one, a fair allocation of the remaining global carbon budget based on the C40 cities methodology already discussed.
Alignment with the IPCC emission reduction targets to reduce warming at 1.5 degrees Celsius.
Integration of the carbon budget with the financial budget, so that the climate impact in terms of terms of GHGs is considered during every decision that the city makes during budget time.
And finally, expectation that every business unit is expected to estimate the GHG impact of initiatives and stay within their budget.
If they do not, they must explain those variances and make corrections in other areas or years to make it up.
Implementing a carbon budgeting approach is expected to have numerous benefits.
The budget would build carbon literacy across the corporation ensuring better understanding of climate mitigation and the impacts of actions.
A carbon budget would increase accountability for meeting established targets once integrated with the financial budgeting process.
It would also help increase transparency and how activities are impacting emissions, meaning less risk of missing targets.
It would also support the city strategic planning work by supplying relevant data to help inform priorities and make decisions on the right initiatives to pursue.
Promoting with city was a meaningful indicator to assess and support progress on the strategic plan.
Of course, there are some implications to consider before implementing a carbon budget.
It will cost both time and money, the development of an accounting framework which is integrated with the financial budgeting process would require assistance from a consulting firm.
A capital funding for its implementation and rate it would require resources from all across the corporation since it will be a transformational shift from how we currently make budget decisions.
It may also give staff and the community the perception that the LEC plan actions are no longer valid.
However, this is not the case.
As the original actions within the LEC plan are still required to reduce emissions, the carbon budget may highlight that the timeline for implementation.
It needs to be accelerated to align with updated IPCC warming thresholds and targets.
